title: The first hard drive weighed over a ton and held 5 million characters
body: IBM announced the 305 RAMAC on 14 September 1956, the first commercial computer with a moving-head hard disk. Its IBM 350 disk unit stacked **fifty 24-inch platters** holding 5 million characters, about as much text as a small stack of novels, and two access arms could reach any record in about 600 milliseconds. The unit weighed over a ton, was moved around by forklift and delivered by cargo plane, and the system leased for $3,200 a month. More than 1,000 were built. According to a later Hitachi executive, the drive could have held more than its roughly five megabytes, but IBM’s marketing department did not know how to sell more storage.

slides.question: How much did IBM charge per month to lease a RAMAC system in 1956?
slides.explanation: US$3,200 a month, equivalent to about $36,700 in 2025. More than 1,000 systems were built before production ended in 1961.

slides.label: spinning 24-inch disks inside the IBM 350 disk unit
slides.text: Two access arms moved up and down to pick a disk and in and out to pick a track, reaching a record in about 600 milliseconds.

slides.heading: Why not bigger?
slides.text: Currie Munce of Hitachi, which later bought IBM’s disk business, said the unit weighed over a ton, moved by forklift and flew in cargo planes. Its capacity could have gone beyond five megabytes, but marketing did not know how to sell a product with more storage.

slides.question: What held the RAMAC’s capacity to about five megabytes, according to Currie Munce?
options: The disks could not spin faster
slides.explanation: IBM’s marketing department was against a larger drive because they did not know how to sell a product with more storage.
